title: Cities and neuroscience research: A systematic literature review
review_question: To explore empirical studies investigating neural mechanisms underlying cognitive and emotional processes elicited by exposure to different urban built and natural spaces, identify new research questions, and leverage neurourbanism for healthier and sustainable cities.
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Included: empirical studies, human adult populations (healthy or diseased), focus on urban built or natural environments influencing objective brain activity (fMRI, fNIRS, PET, EEG, MEG), peer-reviewed, English language. Excluded: abstracts, conference proceedings, opinion/review articles, studies on building interiors, structural imaging only, studies not measuring brain activity, studies with only psychophysiological measurements (heart rate, skin conductance, pupil detection, eye tracking).

findings.antecedent: exposure to urban built environments (pictures of built infrastructures, tall buildings)
findings.source: Functional magnetic resonance studies
findings.quote: urban scenery (with greater suffocating and accustomed self-ratings) elicited more activity in temporal regions (anterior temporal pole, hippocampus, and parahippocampal gyrus), occipital cortex (predominantly the middle occipital gyrus) and amygdala.

findings.antecedent: exposure to natural environments (pictures of natural parks, forests, mountains)
findings.source: Functional magnetic resonance studies
findings.quote: frontal (particularly in the superior and middle frontal gyrus), parietal (in the superior parietal gyrus), precuneus and anterior cingulate cortex regions were the ones more active for the natural setting

findings.antecedent: exposure to natural environments (compared to urban scenes)
findings.source: Functional magnetic resonance-based studies comparing urban built and natural exposure
findings.quote: a walk in the natural setting significantly reduced the neural activity in sgPFC (and independently of the walk-related physiological activations).

findings.antecedent: exposure to natural environments (compared to urban scenes)
findings.source: Functional magnetic resonance-based studies comparing urban built and natural exposure
findings.quote: a walk in the natural setting significantly reduced the neural activity in sgPFC (and independently of the walk-related physiological activations).

findings.antecedent: urban green space (UGS) exposure (GIS-quantified)
findings.source: Functional magnetic resonance-based studies focused predominantly on exposure to natural environments
findings.quote: found a significant within-subject positive correlation between emotional well-being (assessed with a smartphone-based electronic diary) and the GIS-quantified UGS exposure during seven consecutive days.

findings.antecedent: environmental diversity (number of unique locations visited daily)
findings.source: Functional magnetic resonance-based studies focused predominantly on exposure to natural environments
findings.quote: found such positive location-affect relationship, but they also observed that this effect was stronger for those individuals who exhibited a stronger functional connectivity between the ventral striatum and hippocampus

findings.antecedent: current city living (high population density)
findings.source: Functional magnetic resonance-based studies related to urban upbringing and current city-living
findings.quote: Significant differences for the level of current city living were found in the amygdala, which increased stepwise from rural to small towns, and being the highest for city dwellers.

findings.antecedent: urban upbringing (childhood)
findings.consequent: peri-genual anterior cingulate cortex activity (social stress regulation)
findings.source: Functional magnetic resonance-based studies related to urban upbringing and current city-living
findings.quote: urban upbringing was rather associated with the activity in peri-genual anterior cingulate cortex (also increasing linearly with the highest activation for participants raised entirely in the city environment; and lowest for those brought up in rural areas).

findings.antecedent: low-urban upbringing
findings.consequent: amygdala activation (during cooperative investment in trust game)
findings.source: Functional magnetic resonance-based studies related to urban upbringing and current city-living
findings.quote: Low-urban upbringing could be a protective factor for cooperation, which then increases trust related to positive feedback, and this is reflected on amygdala activation.

findings.antecedent: exposure to natural environments (images/videos)
findings.source: Indoor functional near-infrared spectroscopy-based studies comparing urban built and natural exposure
findings.quote: Viewing images of nature, not only increased self-reporting of comfort and relaxation, but it also reduced the activity in the right orbitofrontal cortex

findings.antecedent: exposure to natural environments (forest walk)
findings.source: Functional near-infrared spectroscopy-based studies performed outdoor
findings.quote: The results for the forest walk corroborated the reduced activation in pre-frontal areas.

findings.antecedent: exposure to natural environments (images/videos)
findings.source: Indoor electroencephalography-based studies comparing urban built and natural exposure
findings.quote: imagery of different natural environments-with water and vegetation-elicited higher mean alpha values than built environment photographs.

findings.antecedent: exposure to urban built environments (passive oddball viewing task)
findings.source: Indoor electroencephalography-based studies comparing urban built and natural exposure
findings.quote: built environments elicited a significantly greater LPP activity than natural environments-supporting the views that the latter context leads to better perceived pleasantness

findings.antecedent: exposure to urban scenery (EEG, compared to natural scenery)
findings.source: Indoor electroencephalography-based studies comparing urban built and natural exposure
findings.quote: urban scenery (when compared to different types of natural scenery... elicited a temporally complex signal: with sustained early posterior negativity... followed by an increased P3 component, potentially reflecting some higher allocation of resources or cognitive load

findings.antecedent: presence of people in urban/natural landscape (EEG)
findings.source: Indoor electroencephalography-based studies comparing urban built and natural exposure
findings.quote: a significant 'Landscape type' x 'Human presence' interaction effect was observed.

findings.antecedent: exposure to natural environments (bamboo grove, elderly population)
findings.source: Indoor electroencephalography-based studies focused predominantly on exposure to natural environments
findings.quote: confirmed the previously described increased alpha waves for natural environments observed in young adults.

findings.antecedent: walking in natural outdoor environment (compared to recreational building space)
findings.consequent: theta waves (frontal cortex) and alpha levels (occipital regions)
findings.source: Indoor electroencephalography-based studies focused predominantly on exposure to natural environments
findings.quote: revealed significantly increased theta waves in the frontal cortex and stronger alpha levels in occipital regions-also considered a more 'meditative state'-for the outdoor sessions

findings.antecedent: exposure to green façades (compared to white wall)
findings.source: Electroencephalography-based studies performed outdoor
findings.quote: authors found a significant increase in alpha waves for the frontal and occipital regions when participants were exposed to a façade with climbing plants as opposed to a white wall.

findings.antecedent: walking in green space (elderly population, compared to urban busy street)
findings.source: Electroencephalography-based studies performed outdoor
findings.quote: participants had EEG signals compatible with a reduced attentional effort (using an algorithm and not the raw signal data) while walking in a green space versus an urban busy (and with more built environment) street.

findings.antecedent: walking in green areas (compared to urban areas)
findings.source: Electroencephalography-based studies performed outdoor
findings.quote: Participants showed greater frontal alpha activity when walking in the bamboo forest (and compared to the city walk), an observation that is in line with other studies where walking in green areas induced a mental state of relaxation

findings.antecedent: walking in highly populated urban green spaces (compared to sitting in isolation)
findings.source: Electroencephalography-based studies performed outdoor
findings.quote: participants had a greater frontal beta/alpha ratio for sitting (versus walking) in such green areas-interpreted as a proxy for being more nervous and stressed

findings.antecedent: walking in green spaces (compared to sitting)
findings.source: Electroencephalography-based studies performed outdoor
findings.quote: walking groups had lower beta/alpha ratio (also with more self-reports of positive valence and meditation-like experience) as compared to the sitting group.

findings.antecedent: exposure to urban built artifacts
findings.source: Discussion
findings.quote: The urban built environment (such as buildings, city traffic scenarios, etc.) is commonly regarded as more demanding from a cognitive perspective

findings.antecedent: exposure to urban built stimuli (complex architectural geometry, optical dynamics)
findings.consequent: fMRI activation in brain areas for visual processing, episodic/semantic memory, spatial navigation, object recognition, fear, and stress
findings.source: Discussion
findings.quote: the urban built stimuli elicited greater fMRI activation in brain areas involved in higher-order visual processing... episodic/semantic memory, spatial navigation and object recognition... and in both fear and stress-related responses-the amygdala.

findings.antecedent: exposure to natural environments
findings.consequent: brain activation in areas for basic visual processing, visuospatial perception, sensorial integration, emotional/cognitive control, and motivational behavior
findings.source: Discussion
findings.quote: exposure to nature elicited brain activation in areas more related to basic visual processing (cuneus), visuospatial perception (superior parietal gyrus), sensorial integration (insula), emotional or cognitive control (including the anterior cingulate cortex and the precuneus) and motivational behavior (basal ganglia).

findings.antecedent: urban density
findings.consequent: anxiety, stress, loss of perceived control, increased risk for mental health
findings.source: Discussion
findings.quote: Urban density has been associated to anxiety, stress, loss of perceived control and increased risk for mental health

findings.antecedent: overcrowding
findings.consequent: feelings of violation of personal space, amygdala activation (fear response, negative affect)
findings.source: Discussion
findings.quote: Overcrowding can be felt as a social stressor, inducing feelings of violation of the personal space and activation of amygdala areas linked to fear response and negative affect

findings.antecedent: environmental enrichment
findings.consequent: explorative behavior, self-reported positive affect, reward processing brain regions
findings.source: Discussion
findings.quote: environmental enrichment seemed to incentive explorative behavior and self-reported positive affect, which also involves reward processing brain regions

synthesis_conclusions: Urban built environments elicit greater perceptual, attentional, and spatial cognitive demands, activating brain regions related to visual processing, memory, fear, and stress.
Natural environments promote restorative processes, increasing activation in frontal, parietal, precuneus, anterior cingulate cortex, and basal ganglia, and reducing rumination and sgPFC activity.

Urban upbringing and current city living are associated with increased amygdala and peri-genual anterior cingulate cortex activity, linking to social stress processing and potential mental health risks.
Environmental diversity is crucial for positive affect and well-being, mediated by hippocampal-striatal functional connectivity.
Green and blue spaces, and bio-diverse urban areas, are important for positive neural, cognitive, and emotional processes.
Spatial perception in social contexts (e.g., city overcrowding) deserves further attention for urban planners and scientists.
evidence_gaps: Greater focus on underlying processes bridging urban environmental exposure and mental health/well-being.
More interventional and longitudinal studies to establish causal conclusions.
More studies using clinical populations to generate stronger evidence-based recommendations.
More work on elderly populations and those in initial stages of dementia.
Further exploration of vulnerable groups (migrants, minorities) and gender differences.
Studies comparing limitations and trade-offs of indoor vs. outdoor experimental settings.
Attempts to obtain multimodal data (e.g., EEG-fMRI) for validation.
Incorporation of socio-economic factors (social network, educational background) and individual aspects (personality traits, baseline stress/anxiety) when interpreting neural responses.
Better understanding of long-term effects of childhood upbringing.
risk_of_bias_assessment: Quality assessed using a standard quality assessment criterion (40) on fourteen criteria, scored independently by two authors (0=no, 1=partial, 2=yes). Disagreements resolved by discussion. Kappa score of 78% for internal validation.
heterogeneity_sources: Short exposure time for tested conditions
Lack of combined sensorial modalities in indoor studies
Use of proprietary algorithms for EEG analysis (not raw signals)
Impact of potential confounding variables (noise exposure, social interactions, personality traits, other context variables) frequently disregarded.

moderators.effect: modulates the impact of city living on amygdala and peri-genual anterior cingulate cortex activity, and interacts with dopamine gene patterns to affect prefrontal function.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Higher-urban patients showed a stronger left amygdala reduction of activation than lower-urban patients during cooperative investment; urban childhood upbringing interacted with dopamine gene patterns to affect cerebral responses.

moderators.effect: elicits systematic dose-dependent changes in brain activity (vPCC and cuneus) and stress-ratings.
modulates alpha and beta frequencies in response to urban/natural landscapes.
modulates neurophysiological signatures (beta/alpha ratio) during walking/sitting in urban green spaces.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Walking in a highly populated area and sitting in isolation showed better neurophysiological signatures.

limitations: Potential exclusion of relevant work focused on architecture and interior design (not urban planning/design).
No meta-analysis performed to obtain greater accuracy or improve effect sizes.
Search did not include studies from the last year or non-English publications.
Did not include other important city environmental factors (pollution, noise, temperature).
Only direct brain measurements considered, neglecting indirect biometric stress/emotional assessments.
Imbalance in gender (more males) and age (preference for young) in participants.
Few studies focused on clinical populations or had longitudinal designs.
Short exposure time for tested conditions and simplicity of stimuli (predominantly images).
Few attempts to combine different sensorial modalities in indoor studies.
Several outdoor studies using EEG did not follow conventional neurophysiological analytics (proprietary algorithms).
Frequent disregard of potential confounding variables (noise exposure, social interactions, personality traits, other context variables).

paper_metadata.title: Cities and neuroscience research: A systematic literature review
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Cities and neuroscience research: A systematic literature review
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: BackgroundCities are becoming the socio-economic hubs for most of the world’s population. Understanding how our surroundings can mentally affect everyday life has become crucial to integrate environmental sustainability into urban development. The present review aims to explore the empirical studies investigating neural mechanisms underlying cognitive and emotional processes elicited by the exposure to different urban built and natural spaces. It also tries to identify new research questions and to leverageneurourbanismas a framework to achieve healthier and sustainable cities.MethodsBy following the PRISMA framework, we conducted a structured search on PubMed, ProQuest, Web of Science, and Scopus databases. Only articles related to how urban environment–built or natural–affects brain activity through objective measurement (with either imaging or electrophysiological techniques) were considered. Further inclusion criteria were studies on human adult populations, peer-reviewed, and in English language.ResultsSixty-two articles met the inclusion criteria. They were qualitatively assessed and analyzed to determine the main findings and emerging concepts. Overall, the results suggest that urban built exposure (when compared to natural spaces) elicit activations in brain regions or networks strongly related to perceptual, attentional, and (spatial) cognitive demands. The city’s-built environment also triggers neural circuits linked to stress and negative affect. Convergence of these findings was observed across neuroscience techniques, and for both laboratory and real-life settings. Additionally, evidence also showed associations between neural social stress processing with urban upbringing or current city living–suggesting a mechanistic link to certain mood and anxiety disorders. Finally, environmental diversity was found to be critical for positive affect and individual well-being.ConclusionContemporary human-environment interactions and planetary challenges imply greater understanding of the neurological underpinnings on how the urban space affects cognition and emotion. This review provides scientific evidence that could be applied for policy making on improved urban mental health. Several studies showed that high-quality green or blue spaces, and bio-diverse urban areas, are important allies for positive neural, cognitive, and emotional processes. Nonetheless, the spatial perception in social contexts (e.g., city overcrowding) deserves further attention by urban planners and scientists. The implications of these observations for some theories in environmental psychology and research are discussed. Future work should take advantage of technological advancements to better characterize behavior, brain physiology, and environmental factors and apply them to the remaining complexity of contemporary cities.
